name: The Grumblethorpe Ginkgo
access: Grumblethorpe is run by the Philadelphia Society for the Preservation of Landmarks. Search-result summaries of PhilaLandmarks, Historic Germantown and Schuylkill River Greenways pages give open hours noon to 4 pm on the second Saturday of the month (April or May to October), garden hours 10 am to 12 pm in August to October, tours by appointment, general admission about $10; the sources disagree on months and fee, check philalandmarks.org/contact-visit or 215-843-4820 (hours not read from a fetched page). Whether the ginkgo is seen from Germantown Avenue is not established.

Dating to around 1830, we believe this is one of the oldest female Ginkgo trees in America.' story:
The people who run Grumblethorpe believe the ginkgo in its grounds is one of the oldest female ginkgoes in America.

Ginkgoes come as separate male and female trees, and only the females fruit. Philadelphia's famous one, at Bartram's Garden, is a male planted in 1785. This is the other half of the story. The Philadelphia Society for the Preservation of Landmarks, which owns the house, calls it a massive fruiting ginkgo that towers over the property and dates it to around 1830. The Philadelphia Orchard Project names the man who planted it, Charles Wister Sr., and goes a step further, saying it may be the oldest known living female ginkgo in the country.

Both accounts say circa 1830, and other dates circulate, so take roughly 190 years as an estimate rather than a record. Nobody has published its girth or height.

The tree grew up with a family of gardeners. John Wister built the house in 1744, later Wisters were botanists, and by the owner's account the climbing wisteria is named for them. Grumblethorpe now sits inside the Colonial Germantown Historic District.

Seeing it takes planning. The house opens on a limited schedule, and the published hours, months and admission fee do not agree with each other, so check with the Landmarks society before you go. The pin marks the house, not the trunk, and it is not established whether the tree can be seen from Germantown Avenue.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its size, a fruiting ginkgo that towers over the whole property, with fan-shaped leaves. It stands in the grounds of Grumblethorpe, the 1744 Wister house at 5267 Germantown Avenue.

best_time.label: late October and November, when the fan-shaped leaves turn gold

name: The Penn Treaty Elm on College Green

location.address: College Green, in front of College Hall, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA 19104

access: Free. College Green is open campus lawn between College Hall and 34th Street, reached from Locust Walk; no entry needed.
verify_notes: Penn Today 'The stories trees tell' (2021-04-20, fetched): '1896: Year the University's Penn Treaty elm was planted'. Penn Sustainability page (fetched): 'the Penn Treaty Elm, our oldest and most famous tree on campus'; its photo caption places it in College Green. Penn Today history feature (2017-10-11, fetched) says the 'iconic Treaty Elm' was planted in front of College Green in the late 1800s/early 1900s greening. Planting date documented for THIS specimen, so about 130 years (range 125-135). Lineage: the name refers to the Shackamaxon/Penn Treaty Elm (under which William Penn is said to have treated with the Lenape; original felled in a storm in 1810 at Penn Treaty Park, Kensington). Wikipedia's cultivar article (fetched) says the 'Penn Treaty' clone came from an 1840 Haverford graft of the original; it does NOT say how Penn's 1896 tree descends, and a search summary (not a fetched page) says Penn calls it a descendant: state as named for / reputed descendant, no more. Dutch elm disease is an ongoing risk per a search summary of Penn (not fetched). Alive: Penn pages from 2021 and later list it standing; no dated trunk observation, lifecheck not run. No girth/height found (monumentaltrees has a record, not used). Pin: College Hall (OSM way 51367353, 39.9515,-75.1938) shifted to the green east of it; NOT tree-level, approximate. Flagged: approximate pin, lineage unsourced on Penn's side. Cluster: about 1.2 km from The Woodlands (phl_006), about 3 km from Bartram's Garden (phl_001, phl_005) (straight-line estimates).
story:
William Penn is said to have made his treaty with the Lenape under a great elm in Kensington. A storm brought that tree down in 1810. The University of Pennsylvania has kept the name alive on its own lawn ever since 1896.

That year Penn planted an American elm on College Green, in front of College Hall, and called it the Penn Treaty Elm. The university's sustainability office now calls it the oldest and most famous tree on campus. At about 130 years it is not ancient, but unlike most old trees its planting year is written down.

The name is the interesting part, and also the uncertain one. A Penn Treaty clone of the original is traced to a graft made at Haverford in 1840, and Penn is reported to describe its own tree as a descendant. None of the university pages we could read spells out that line of descent, so treat it as a reputed descendant, named for the Treaty Elm, rather than a proven child of it.

It went in during the campus greening of the late 1800s, and it has watched the university build up around the lawn since. Elms in America live under the shadow of Dutch elm disease, and this one is no exception.

Getting to it costs nothing. College Green is open lawn between College Hall and 34th Street, reached from Locust Walk. The pin is approximate, set on the green rather than on the trunk.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the old American elm on College Green, Penn's oldest campus tree. It stands on the lawn in front of College Hall, between the hall and 34th Street, off Locust Walk.

name: The Tabletop Scotch Elm at Morris Arboretum

location.address: Morris Arboretum & Gardens, 100 E Northwestern Ave, Philadelphia, PA 19118 (Morris Pond cluster)

official_register.name: Morris Arboretum & Gardens Great Trees list (owner)

access: Paid entry to Morris Arboretum & Gardens (adults $22, seniors $20, youth $12, children 2 and under free, per the arboretum's site in Nov 2026); open daily, hours on the arboretum's site.
verify_notes: ONE SOURCE (owner of the ground): Morris Arboretum's own blog 'Plant Names and Provenance' (Katherine Wagner-Reiss, 1 Nov 2023) says the tree was planted by the Morrises on the Morris Estate sometime before 1909, accessioned 1932 (the year the estate was bequeathed to the University of Pennsylvania), and calls it over a century old; the Great Trees page lists it in the 'Morris Pond Cluster' beside a Chinese elm, and the same page lists a Weeping European beech planted before 1909 by the Morrises. Alive: the 2023 blog describes it in present tense and the Great Trees page (copyright 2026) still lists it; no dated photo or observation within the last year seen, so flagged. Age: 'before 1909' gives a minimum of about 117 years only (1909 to 2026); max 139 is NOT sourced beyond the Morrises buying the property in 1887 when it was almost treeless (per the arboretum's history page), so treat 117 to 139 as a broad bracket, not a date; the 1816 date in the blog is the cultivar's origin (a seedling in a nursery at Perth, Scotland), not this tree. What makes it remarkable: a grafted tree, the weeping scion of a procumbent elm grafted high onto a 7-foot understock, forming a flat umbrella or table-like top; the graft scar is visible; the blog says the arboretum is one of very few in the US to grow one; it is as susceptible to Dutch elm disease as any elm; yellow fall colour. Recognition: flat-topped horizontal crown on a ~7 ft (about 2.1 m) trunk with a visible graft union, by Morris Pond. Pin: arboretum-level (the same garden coordinate as the other Morris entries); the Great Trees tour PDF map (morrisarboretum.org/sites/default/files/2023-01/tours-great-trees.pdf) numbers the trees but its text could not be read by script, so the exact spot at Morris Pond is not placed. Never a walk-through garden as a small site, so no location_site. No girth or height given by any source. Not in the NW Philadelphia city file; sits within a few metres of phl_003, phl_004, phl_020 and phl_021 for walking purposes (same garden).
story:
This elm is two trees on one trunk, and you can still see where they were joined. Some time before 1909 the Morris family planted it on their Chestnut Hill estate. It is a low, sprawling elm grafted high onto a straight understock about seven feet up, so the branches spread out flat and hang at the edges like a table top on a single leg.

The form is older than the tree. It began in 1816 as one odd seedling in a nursery at Perth, in Scotland. The arboretum says it is one of very few in the United States to grow one. A tabletop elm is as open to Dutch elm disease as any other elm. This one is still standing.

The estate passed to the University of Pennsylvania in 1932, the year the tree was entered in the arboretum's records, and it stands in the Morris Pond group beside a Chinese elm. In autumn the flat crown turns yellow.

Our only source for it is the arboretum itself, and the newest description we have dates from 2023, so if you have seen it lately, tell us. Entry is paid, and the pin marks the arboretum rather than the tree, so head for the pond.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the flat, table-like crown on a trunk about 2 metres tall, with the graft scar showing where the two meet. It stands by Morris Pond, beside a Chinese elm.
